title: NXP UCODE 8 — UHF Chip Technical Encyclopedia (Memory, Commands, Cost Profile, Deployment)
summary: UCODE 8 (NXP SL3S1203 / SL3S1213) has been the cost-of-gravity UHF inlay chip since its 2017 launch. Shipping in billions of units per year, it powers the majority of promotional, event, single-use and cost-sensitive UHF deployments still converting today. This encyclopedia documents UCODE 8's memory layout, EPC Gen2 v2 command support, sensitivity envelope, the UCODE 8 versus UCODE 8m distinction, and the specific deployment classes where UCODE 8 remains the correct choice in 2026 even as UCODE 9 takes the sensitivity crown.
heroPoints: Industry cost anchor — UCODE 8 is the reference chip against which every other UHF chip's price is benchmarked. At strap-volume orders the per-unit chip cost is approximately half a US cent, making it the only silicon that works economically for billion-unit-per-year promotional and supply-chain programs.

EPC Gen2 v2 support — Untraceable and Authenticate commands are present (though simpler than UCODE 9), providing forward compatibility with EU retail privacy requirements at the cost-optimized end of the market.

Two variants — UCODE 8 (SL3S1203, 128-bit EPC memory, no user memory) and UCODE 8m (SL3S1213, 96-bit EPC + 32-bit user memory). Both are factory-interchangeable from a reader perspective; the variant decision is driven purely by whether the application needs the 32 bits of user memory.

sections.title: Family and part numbers
bullets: UCODE 8 — NXP part number SL3S1203. 128-bit EPC, no user memory. Optimized for applications where the EPC itself carries all the identity information (SGTIN-96, SGTIN-128, SSCC-96) and no additional item-specific data needs to live on the tag.

UCODE 8m — NXP part number SL3S1213. 96-bit EPC plus 32 bits of user memory. Same chip architecture and sensitivity; the added user memory provides space for a backup serial, a factory lot code or an authentication password salt.

UCODE 8xm — NXP part number SL3S1215. Extended variant with 96-bit EPC plus 128 bits of user memory. Less common in production; where UCODE 8xm's memory is called for, projects often jump directly to UCODE 9xm for sensitivity reasons.

Strap and inlay availability — UCODE 8 has been shipped by every major strap vendor (Smartrac, Avery Dennison, Arizon, Neology, SATO) in a full range of standard reference-design inlays: Dogbone, Frog 3D, AD-383u7 apparel inlay, AD-Minute small-format, PaperTag — all produced and still sold for cost-sensitive programs.
Operating temperature — -40 °C to +85 °C normal, peak 125 °C for short excursions. Not suitable for tire-cure or sustained autoclave applications.

Counterfeit watch — authentic UCODE 8 returns TID = 0xE28011xxx (NXP mask ID) with model-ID bits indicating UCODE 8 (0x070 for SL3S1203, 0x050 for SL3S1213). Clones often present as 'UCODE 8 compatible' but return an unknown or zero model ID.

sections.title: Memory architecture
bullets: Four standard EPC Gen2 memory banks. Bank 00 = Reserved (kill and access passwords, 32 bits each). Bank 01 = EPC bank. Bank 10 = TID bank. Bank 11 = User memory bank.
EPC memory bank 01 — on UCODE 8 (SL3S1203), extended to 128 bits, making it suitable for longer identifiers without dipping into other banks. On UCODE 8m (SL3S1213), 96 bits standard EPC.
TID memory bank 10 — 96 bits read-only, factory-programmed. Uniqueness across the entire UCODE 8 population is guaranteed by the manufacturing process.
User memory bank 11 — 0 bits on SL3S1203, 32 bits on SL3S1213, 128 bits on SL3S1215. The user memory is always aligned at bit 0 of bank 11 and addressable in 16-bit words.
Kill and Access passwords — 32 bits each, factory default all-zeros, writeable in bank 00 by a Gen2 Write or BlockWrite command after a successful Req_RN / Access exchange.
Write endurance — 100,000 writes per location. Data retention ≥ 10 years at 55 °C (per NXP data sheet) and ≥ 20 years at 25 °C.

sections.title: EPC Gen2 v2 command set as implemented
bullets: Core Gen2 commands — Query, QueryAdjust, QueryRep, ACK, NAK, Req_RN, Read, Write, Kill, Lock, Access, BlockWrite, BlockErase, BlockPermalock, BlockReadEx. UCODE 8 is fully v2 compliant for the core set.

Untraceable — supported on both SL3S1203 and SL3S1213. When activated, the tag shortens its EPC response to a non-unique pattern and restricts TID access. Useful for EU retail privacy compliance; syntax identical to UCODE 9's Untraceable.

Authenticate — supported, with a 64-bit challenge-response. The implementation on UCODE 8 is the lightweight variant specified in GS1 Gen2 v2 Section 6.3.2.10 (short-form Authenticate) rather than the extended form on UCODE 9; for most deployments both are sufficient.
Challenge — supported.

File Open / File Privilege — partially supported. UCODE 8m exposes one file (the user-memory bank) with a per-file access password. UCODE 8 (SL3S1203, no user memory) does not expose the File mechanism meaningfully.

Not supported on UCODE 8 but available on UCODE 9 — the crypto suite 0x00 02 (stronger HMAC variant), some of the File Privilege fine-grained modes, and the Self-Adjust Sensitivity calibration command. Applications needing these features should specify UCODE 9.
Anti-collision performance — ~500 tags/sec sustained in Dense-Reader Mode at 640 kbps. Sufficient for retail POS and logistics portal throughput.

sections.title: Read sensitivity and read-range expectations
bullets: Forward-link sensitivity -19 dBm (reference inlay, free-air, ISO/IEC 18046-3 conditions). About 5 dB less sensitive than UCODE 9 and 2-3 dB less than Monza R6.
Backscatter sensitivity -15 dBm. Again the practical limit is set by the reader, not the chip; UCODE 8 keeps up with any commercial reader at typical retail and logistics distances.

Practical read range — ~6-8 m on a reference dipole inlay at 30 dBm reader output. Shorter than UCODE 9 and Monza R6, but adequate for the applications UCODE 8 is typically used in (POS item-level, event wristbands, promotional inserts).

Temperature sensitivity — stable from -40 °C to +85 °C; beyond 85 °C the forward-link sensitivity degrades approximately 0.05 dB per degree C. Not a concern for retail or indoor-industrial deployments.

Antenna match — chip impedance at 915 MHz is approximately 11-j120 ohms. Most commercial UCODE 8 dipoles target 11+j120 for maximum power transfer. The majority of reference inlay designs in circulation are tuned for UCODE 8's impedance rather than UCODE 9's.

sections.title: When UCODE 8 is the right choice in 2026
bullets: Billion-unit promotional campaigns — event tickets, conference badges, single-use retail inserts, festival wristbands. Cost dominates; the tag's life is measured in days or a single use. UCODE 9's sensitivity upgrade doesn't justify the 30-50% cost premium at the scale these programs operate.

Library RFID replacement inlays — existing deployments with millions of UCODE 8 tags in circulation continue to specify UCODE 8 for replacement inlays to maintain read consistency across the installed base.
Transport ticketing — mass-transit disposable fare cards and event venue ticket strips. Read range requirements are modest (10-20 cm at a gate reader); UCODE 8's performance envelope is comfortable.

Asset-labeling programs where the reader network is already sized for UCODE 8 — upgrading mid-program to UCODE 9 often introduces unintended read-rate variance that can complicate portal calibration. Consistency across the tag population matters more than per-tag maximum range.

Supply-chain tertiary packaging — outer carton and pallet tags where the read distance is short (dock-door portal <2 m tag-to-antenna) and cost scales with the number of cartons. UCODE 8 at sub-cent cost is appropriate.

When UCODE 8 is wrong — retail POS portals with high read-rate requirements (use UCODE 9), harsh industrial with >85 °C ambient (use Monza R6-P or industrial-rated variants), high-counterfeit-risk brand authentication (use NTAG424 DNA at HF or UCODE DNA at UHF), ultra-long-range yard/warehouse (use Impinj M800 class silicon).

sections.title: UCODE 8 vs UCODE 8m vs UCODE 9 selection
bullets: Need extra memory for a serialized backup? — UCODE 8m (SL3S1213) with 32 bits user memory. Most common for hospitality/linen applications that serialize items at the wash cycle and want a backup on-tag beyond the central database.
Need longer EPC (128-bit SGTIN-198 or similar)? — UCODE 8 (SL3S1203) with 128-bit EPC. Less common; most retailers use 96-bit SGTIN encodings.

Need best-in-class sensitivity for POS portal performance? — UCODE 9 (SL3S4011). UCODE 8's ~5 dB sensitivity gap becomes material at POS gate distances, where the difference between 95% first-pass read and 99% first-pass read determines whether the POS clerk has to manually scan missed items.
Need Untraceable / Authenticate for EU retail privacy? — both UCODE 8m and UCODE 9 support it. Either works. If no other driver, UCODE 8m is the cost-optimal choice.

Need high-temperature tolerance? — neither UCODE 8 nor UCODE 9 is suitable for sustained operation beyond 85 °C. Specify Monza R6-P (for tire-cure) or a UHF chip specifically rated for automotive/industrial temperature ranges.

faq.question: Should I specify UCODE 8 or UCODE 9 for a new retail deployment?
faq.answer: UCODE 9 for new deployments at any meaningful scale. The sensitivity upgrade (~5 dB forward-link, ~7 dB backscatter) pays back in portal read-rate improvement — typically 3-5 percentage points — which is worth far more operationally than the ~30% per-chip cost premium. UCODE 8 remains appropriate for billion-unit promotional and single-use programs where the tag is discarded quickly and per-unit cost dominates the economics.

faq.question: What is the difference between UCODE 8 (SL3S1203) and UCODE 8m (SL3S1213)?
faq.answer: User memory. SL3S1203 has a 128-bit EPC with no user memory — maximum encoding flexibility at the expense of on-tag item-specific data. SL3S1213 has a 96-bit EPC plus 32 bits of user memory, which is the more common choice for applications that want a backup serial, factory lot code or similar item-level metadata on the tag itself. Both chips have identical sensitivity, temperature envelope and command support.

faq.question: Can UCODE 8 be used for EU retail deployments that require privacy compliance?
faq.answer: Yes. UCODE 8 supports the EPC Gen2 v2 Untraceable command, which when activated at the POS shortens the tag's response to a non-unique pattern, giving the customer privacy after the item leaves the store. Syntax is the same as UCODE 9. For retailers where UHF RFID is a 2024+ deployment, UCODE 9 is the more common specification for new inlay runs, but UCODE 8 with Untraceable satisfies the privacy requirement at lower cost.

faq.question: How do I detect counterfeit chips being sold as UCODE 8?
faq.answer: Read the full 96-bit TID. Authentic UCODE 8 returns: first 16 bits = 0xE280 (EPC class identifier + NXP mask designer ID), next 12 bits = 0x070 (SL3S1203) or 0x050 (SL3S1213) mask IDs, remaining 64 bits = per-chip unique serial. Chinese-OEM clones frequently return an incorrect model ID or return all-zeros in the mask-designer field. Incoming-inspection scripts should verify the TID pattern and cross-reference with NXP's published mask-ID registry.

faq.question: Does UCODE 8 work on metal surfaces?
faq.answer: Only with a dedicated anti-metal inlay design — typically 0.5-1 mm PET or ferrite spacer. Standard UCODE 8 inlays laminated directly onto metal detune to the point of non-functionality. Proud Tek stocks anti-metal UCODE 8 variants for cost-sensitive applications; for performance-critical metal applications (automotive assembly, mining assets) use Monza R6 or Monza R6-P on a reference anti-metal antenna.

faq.question: What is the longest EPC I can encode on UCODE 8 (SL3S1203)?
faq.answer: 128 bits, which accommodates SGTIN-96 (96 bits), SSCC-96 (96 bits), GIAI-96 (96 bits), SGTIN-198 truncated forms, or a custom 128-bit company-private encoding. The 128-bit EPC bank lets you encode longer identifiers than the 96-bit-only variants without dipping into user memory (which SL3S1203 doesn't have).

faq.question: Is UCODE 8 still in production, or has NXP EOL'd it?
faq.answer: Still in production in 2026. UCODE 8 ships in volumes measured in tens of billions of units per year globally, and NXP has signaled continued production through at least 2028. UCODE 9 is the successor for high-sensitivity applications but does not displace UCODE 8 at the cost-optimized end of the market.
